turn_text: Yeah, this was very fortuitous set of circumstances this year for us to finally get that across the finish line. My father initiated that effort. It really started when he was the government teacher at South San Francisco High School. He would often Yet his kids involved in local city council meetings and school board meetings, and I think he would give them extra credit if they got involved in any particular city council campaign. He never steered them in one direction or the other and never steered them certainly from a partisan standpoint. But he really wanted to encourage young people to get involved in civic affairs and in local government in particular. Local government is where he really believes that young people could have a direct impact and they could see the impact of their efforts. So that started him thinking about what are some other ways to get young people engaged early in voting and in politics and maybe that kind of fires their interests and aspirations themselves. So he took that classroom experience when he came to the Capitol and introduced the ACA a number of times. He did it at least twice. Some of his colleagues stepped up and sort of carried that. baton forward and then I've tried it myself a couple of different times so we finally this year we're able to garner the two-thirds vote in both the assembly and the senate to put it on the ballot and what's sort of interesting it's actually a little surprising that it's been so hard for that to happen because it's already in place in 18 other states so-called red states and blue states. Some of the most Republican states in the country allow 17-year-olds to vote in the primary. But unfortunately, it got framed in a partisan context for some reason in California. And it's just not a partisan issue. Young people are actually trending toward no-party preference, as a matter of fact. So it's not as though this will be some kind of a boom to the Democratic Party. And I did get bipartisan support. And we were able to get this on the ballot. And the key though I should mention I need to give a shout out to my colleague Evan Lowe, who had his own version of this, which is a straight lowering of the voting age across the board to 17. His effort got held up. He sort of rolled in with my effort. And we've been able to double team now, proposition 18. And that's going to be on the ballot. It's a little interesting numbering of proposition 18 with the 17 year old primary vote. But we're actually using that as an opportunity to remind people that these young people still have to be 18 by the general election. This would just enable them to participate in the primary. Sort of looking at the election as a full-cycle primary and general, which is the way we should be viewing it. But it sort of builds on the pre-registration program that Secretary of State Alex Padilla has put in place, a very successful program. I think close to 200,000 young people have pre-registered. So it's sort of building on those efforts to engage our young people. I'm hoping that it's going to be successful in November, but one, frankly, never really knows how the public is going to view this. I don't have access to any polling or anything like that. I just think it's a modest, reasonable expansion of voting rights for young people, and I'm certainly hoping that it will be successful, and I will be very much involved in the campaign this fall.
